Hanakapiai Beach Hike: A Superb Day on the Kalalau Trail

AffiliateGuide
Author: Alec Sills-Trausch
October 13, 2026October 13, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:21
Instaread

Kauai is full of fantastic hiking trails, but one that rises above is the Kalalau Trail and Hanakapiai Beach hike. Tucked into the island’s northwestern side, the trailhead is as far as the road goes.

From there, you’ll need to rely on your feet to see one of the world’s most magical coastlines: the Na Pali Coast. And my gosh, it’s worth it. On a sunny day, with the water a vibrant blue, the Hanakapiai Beach hike ranks among the country’s best hikes.

If you’re planning your Kauai itinerary, make sure this makes the cut. And if you’re here for another reason, enjoy the trail photos, and hopefully they inspire you to plan a trip to this Hawaiian Island.

Hiking Guide to Hanakapiai Beach on the Kalalau Trail

  • Trail Distance: 4.8 miles RT to the beach, 8 miles to the waterfall
  • Elevation Gain: 1,230 feet of gain (AllTrails is inaccurate)
  • Difficulty: Moderate, but can be quite muddy
  • Time on Trail: 3.5-4.5 hours
  • Trailhead Location: Kalalau Trailhead (but parking here is quite limited); you’ll likely want the Waipa Park & Ride
  • Without a backpacking permit, you can’t go further down the coast
  • Are drones allowed? No.
  • Drink plenty of water

My Trip Report to Hanakapiai Beach

My wife’s family flew out in the morning, while we booked a red-eye back to Seattle. This gave us one final day to see the island and wrap up the last things we wanted to do. And in classic Alec and Jaimie fashion, we used up every ounce of daylight we could.

We also weren’t sure we’d even make it to the Hanakapiai Beach Trail. The previous two days were closed because of muddy conditions. Thankfully, when we woke up, the trail was open. We drove counterclockwise around the island from Poipu to Princeville, a drive that takes about 75 minutes.

I don’t remember what our shuttle time was (we snagged one of the last available ones), but I had read you can get on another bus via standby. So we did! At 11:30, after parking at the Waipa Park and Ride, we were off to explore the Na Pali Coast!

On the Trail

The shuttle drops you off in the parking lot, and we started the first portion of the trail: a nice, flat walk through the forest to Ke’e Beach. From here, the trail begins to rollercoaster, going up and down, up and down, over the two-plus miles to Hanakapiai Beach.

At the half-mile mark, you’ll get a great view of the Na Pali Coast. At the 1.5-mile mark, you’ll get another lovely view down the coastline.

What I remember the most was how freaking muddy it was! Without my waterproof boots or sandals (another muddy hike had ripped off the soles), I was in my trail runners. This meant I was trying my hardest not to soak my feet – at least on the way out.

Down to Hanakapiai Beach

After that final viewpoint, it’s a quick descent to the freshwater creek and then the beach. Some people choose to turn around once they reach the water. For us, we were crossing. I took off my shoes, made sure my camera wouldn’t fall off, and started across.

wouldn’t say it was too challenging at this point, though I’m sure it was flowing faster than at other times (and slower than at other moments).

I doubt it took us more than two minutes to get across, and then we headed under the trees to enjoy lunch and the crashing waves along the rocky shore.

My wife and I would have loved to get up to the Hanakapiai Waterfall (another two miles of harder terrain), but we had a 10pm flight out of Lihue and didn’t want to A) miss the shuttle back to our car and B) miss our flight home to Seattle.

Instead, we relaxed and reminisced about what had been an absolutely memorable trip. We boated along the Na Pali Coast, did a doors-off helicopter flight, snorkeled, saw sea turtles, ate delicious fish, and enjoyed some of the world’s most striking views. Kauai had been so good to us, and it had quickly risen to the top of our favorite places to explore.

Thoughts on the Trail

The trail isn’t that hard. It’s not overly steep, it doesn’t have crazy elevation gain or loss, and doesn’t put you in precarious situations. It is, though, quite muddy, with roots and rocks, and it’s not friendly to those who don’t have good balance.

It can also be hot and humid, so come prepared with sun protection and plenty of water. Additionally, take your time on the uphill. This isn’t a sprint.

Lastly, I know packing hiking poles for vacation is annoying, but I would recommend it for this trail. They’ll help you navigate the muddy sections and cross the water.

What You Need to Know Before Hiking on the Kalalau Trail

Get Your Shuttle Permit in Advance

This is THE most important thing you can do. Without it, you’ll be SOL and likely won’t be able to hike. Click here to get your permit. Click here for the Waipa Park and Ride lot location.

What to know about the reservations:

  • Costs $45 per person for shuttle and entry (ages 16+)
  • Parking at the trailhead is very limited. Don’t bet on that being open. Hawai residents get free access.
  • Opens 30 days prior
  • Passes are non-transferable
  • 10% cancellation fee
  • You can ride standby for a time other than what you selected (we did this)

Confirm Trail is Open

This area gets a lot of rain, and the trail will close if it is deemed too dangerous or unhikable. We went through a rollercoaster of emotions: the trail was closed the day before, and we weren’t sure it would be open on our final day in Kauai. Luckily, it opened, and we had a wonderful time.

Keep an eye on this page for trail updates.

Check Weather Forecast

While Haena State Park will let you know whether the trail will be open or closed for the day, you also need to check the weather forecast. If you make it to Hanakapiai Beach on the Kalalau Trail, you have to cross a decent-sized creek. With heavy rain, this can swell and become impassable.

In recent years, people have been stranded overnight on the far side. If it starts to rain, get across to the trailhead side ASAP.

Have Necessary Hiking Gear

This hike can be very muddy, so plan accordingly. Some people say to bring sandals; others say to hike barefoot; and others say to bring waterproof boots. Honestly, I’m not sure what the right call is. Jaimie tried going barefoot, then ditched the idea after a half mile.

The hard part is, I wasn’t going to pack my LOWAs for a non-hiking trip to Kauai because I had limited room in my suitcase. We did this trail in April 2025, and I wore my trail runners because my Chacos were destroyed on the Secret Falls hike.

  • Hat – either wide-brimmed or this Patagonia style
  • Sunblock
  • Trail Runners – Altra Lone Peaks are my go-to
  • Sun Shirt or sun hoodie – Colder conditions: REI Sahara Shade, Warmer Conditions: Patagonia Capilene, Other good ones: Fjallraven Abisko, Outdoor Research Astroman
  • Hiking Shirt – Patagonia Capilene is my favorite
  • Rain Jacket – Torrentshell 3L Jacket
  • Hiking shorts – Fjallraven or these from Prana
  • Wool hiking socks – Darn Tough is fantastic
  • Sunglasses – Goodr are perfect without breaking the bank
  • Hiking Pack: 15-25 liters is perfect for a day hike – This one’s on the smaller end; here’s a 25L option
  • At least 2L of water, and bring this easy-to-use 1 L filter
  • Snacks and a sandwich – bring something salty to help with sodium replenishment

DO NOT GO INTO THE WATER AT HANAKAPIAI BEACH

Yes, this requires all caps. Hanakapiai Beach is dangerous, and swimming is not recommended. It’s one of the deadliest beaches in Hawaii, with rip currents, violent shore breaks, high surf, very rocky terrain, and no medical assistance.

Stay out of the water.

If you want to swim, do it at the end of your hike at Ke’e Beach. It was super pretty and calm, with good snorkeling. That said, in winter, swells can get bigger, so always confirm safety and use best judgment.

Bring Plenty of Water

Yes, you are hiking next to the ocean. No, that doesn’t mean it’ll be nice and cool. Hiking in Kauai means your hike will be humid and possibly even quite warm. Much of the trail is exposed to the sun, and the humidity will make it feel even hotter.

Carry at least 2L of water, or bring a water filter to refill at the stream.

One thing to note: leptospirosis is a serious bacterial disease in the freshwater along the Na Pali Coast. Avoid entering freshwater with open sores, and don’t drink it untreated. While it’s unlikely you’ll get it, it’s worth knowing.

More photos from our time on the trail

If you need more inspiration for this hike, check out more trail photos.

Final Thoughts on Hiking to Hanakapiai Beach in Kauai

This is a truly fantastic hike. It showcases the beauty of the Na Pali Coast for a fraction of the cost of other tours, whether by air or by boat.

While I’m an avid hiker and found this a pretty moderate hike, don’t discount the challenge if you don’t hike weekly. It can be wet and slippery, or it can be hot, humid, and also slippery. Come prepared, be a good trail steward, and you’ll be just fine!

Until next time, adventurers, stay safe.
